# Aṅgulimāla Sutta (MN 86 (PTS MN ii 97))
**ID:** MN 86 (PTS MN ii 97)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Aṅgulimāla Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** With Aṅgulimāla
**PTS:** MN ii 97
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn86

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Aṅgulimāla Sutta* (MN 86) recounts the Buddha's encounter with and peaceful conversion of the notorious mass-murderer Aṅgulimāla [SuttaCentral; Galasek 2016]. After renouncing violence and receiving ordination as a monk, Aṅgulimāla attains awakening, though he continues to experience residual kammic retribution in the form of physical injuries sustained during alms rounds [SuttaCentral; Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003]. In a famous episode, the Buddha instructs him to assist a woman undergoing a agonizing childbirth by making an "act of truth" (*saccakiriyā*): affirming that since being born into the noble birth of the monastic order, he has never intentionally deprived any living being of life [Gombrich 1991; Langenberg; Crosby 2014]. This declaration safely resolves the delivery, and the formula became established as a widely used protective chant (*paritta*) recited for pregnant women in Theravāda traditions, included in collections such as the *Catubhāṇavārapāḷi* [Appleton 2010; Crosby 2014]. The narrative background is further expounded in Buddhaghosa's commentary, the *Papañcasūdanī* [Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003; Galasek 2016].
A large portion of the sutta's concluding verses corresponds directly to the twenty-six stanzas of the *Aṅgulimālattheragāthā* (Thag 16.8, vv. 871–886), with individual verses shared across the *Dhammapada* and *Udānavarga* [SuttaCentral; Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003; Galasek 2016]. DharmaNexus confirms extensive Pali-internal text reuse with Thag 16.8 (notably §18.3–18.66), as well as formulaic parallels across the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, and the Vinaya Khandhakas [DharmaNexus]. Parallels in other languages include two discourses in the Chinese *Saṃyukta-āgama* (SĀ 1077 and SĀ² 16 / T 100), one in the *Ekottarika-āgama* (EĀ 38.6 / T 125), two standalone Chinese translations (T 118 and T 119), and multiple Sanskrit manuscript fragments (such as SHT sutta2 and SF 19, 66) [SuttaCentral; Langenberg; Meisig 2010]. DharmaNexus also records machine alignments with these Āgama texts and with the Mahāyāna *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* (T 120; Tibetan D 213), though scholars identify the latter as an independent Mahāyāna work distinct from the early canonical versions [Nattier; DharmaNexus].
